Ethinyl Estradiol and Enasidenib: The coadministration of enasidenib may alter the concentrations of combined hormonal contraceptives, but the clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. Close monitoring is recommended. 2. Ethinyl Estradiol and Encorafenib: Encorafenib, a BCRP inhibitor, may increase the concentration and toxicity of BCRP substrates, including ethinyl estradiol. It may also decrease ethinyl estradiol levels by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism, potentially reducing contraceptive efficacy. Alternative nonhormonal contraceptive methods are advised. 3. Ethinyl Estradiol and Enoxaparin: Ethinyl estradiol may reduce the effects of enoxaparin due to pharmacodynamic antagonism, increasing the risk of thromboembolic disorders. This combination is contraindicated. 4. Ethinyl Estradiol and Enzalutamide: Enzalutamide may decrease ethinyl estradiol levels by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Alternative contraceptive methods are recommended. 5. Ethinyl Estradiol and Eplerenone: Ethinyl estradiol may increase eplerenone levels by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. The clinical significance is unclear, but close monitoring is advised. 6. Ethinyl Estradiol and Erythromycin: Erythromycin may decrease ethinyl estradiol levels by altering intestinal flora, which applies only to oral forms of the hormone. The risk of contraceptive failure is low, but caution and monitoring are recommended. 7. Ethinyl Estradiol and Eslicarbazepine Acetate: Eslicarbazepine acetate may reduce ethinyl estradiol levels by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism, potentially compromising contraceptive efficacy. Additional or alternative nonhormonal contraception is advised. 8. Ethinyl Estradiol and Etravirine: Etravirine may decrease ethinyl estradiol levels by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism, reducing contraceptive efficacy. Nonhormonal contraception is recommended. 9. Ethinyl Estradiol and Exemestane: Ethinyl estradiol may antagonize the effects of exemestane. Concurrent use of estrogens or estrogen-containing products with exemestane is not recommended. 10. Ethinyl Estradiol and Exenatide: Exenatide may reduce the absorption of oral contraceptives by slowing gastric emptying. Patients should take oral contraceptives at least one hour before or 11 hours after exenatide administration. 11. Ethinyl Estradiol and Fedratinib: Fedratinib may increase ethinyl estradiol levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution and monitoring are advised. 12. Ethinyl Estradiol and Felbamate: Felbamate may decrease ethinyl estradiol levels through an unknown mechanism. The clinical significance is unclear, but monitoring is recommended. 13. Ethinyl Estradiol and Fexinidazole: Fexinidazole may increase ethinyl estradiol levels by inhibiting CYP2E1 metabolism. Alternative contraceptive methods are recommended. 14. Ethinyl Estradiol and Fezolinetant: Fezolinetant levels may increase when coadministered with ethinyl estradiol due to CYP1A2 inhibition. This combination is contraindicated. 15. Ethinyl Estradiol and Finererone: Ethinyl estradiol may increase finererone levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Serum potassium levels should be monitored, and therapy adjusted as needed. 16. Ethinyl Estradiol and Flibanserin: Flibanserin levels may increase when coadministered with ethinyl estradiol, potentially leading to adverse effects. Monitoring is recommended. 17. Ethinyl Estradiol and Fluconazole: Fluconazole may increase ethinyl estradiol levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution and monitoring are advised. 18. Ethinyl Estradiol and Fluvoxamine: Fluvoxamine may increase ethinyl estradiol levels by inhibiting CYP1A2 metabolism. Monitoring is recommended. 19. Ethinyl Estradiol and Fosamprenavir: Fosamprenavir may alter hormone levels and reduce contraceptive efficacy. Nonhormonal contraceptive methods are recommended. 20. Ethinyl Estradiol and Fostemsavir: Fostemsavir may increase ethinyl estradiol levels by inhibiting BCRP transporters. Hormone doses should not exceed 30 mcg/day. 21. Ethinyl Estradiol and Grapefruit: Grapefruit may increase ethinyl estradiol levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitoring is recommended. 22. Ethinyl Estradiol and Griseofulvin: Griseofulvin may reduce ethinyl estradiol levels by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism, potentially reducing contraceptive efficacy. Nonhormonal contraception is recommended. 23. Ethinyl Estradiol and Heparin: Ethinyl estradiol may antagonize the effects of heparin, increasing the risk of thromboembolic disorders. This combination is contraindicated. 24. Ethinyl Estradiol and Hyaluronidase: Estrogens may reduce the effectiveness of hyaluronidase, requiring higher doses for equivalent effects. 25. Ethinyl Estradiol and Idelalisib: Idelalisib may increase ethinyl estradiol levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Alternative therapies are recommended. 26. Ethinyl Estradiol and Itraconazole: Itraconazole may increase ethinyl estradiol levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitoring is recommended. 27. Ethinyl Estradiol and Ketoconazole: Ketoconazole may increase ethinyl estradiol levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitoring is recommended. 28. Ethinyl Estradiol and Lamotrigine: Ethinyl estradiol may reduce lamotrigine levels by inducing glucuronidation, potentially reducing its efficacy. Monitoring is recommended. 29. Ethinyl Estradiol and Lapatinib: Lapatinib levels may increase when coadministered with ethinyl estradiol. Monitoring is recommended. 30. Ethinyl Estradiol and Letrozole: Letrozole should not be used concurrently with estrogens or estrogen-containing products. 31. Ethinyl Estradiol and Liraglutide: Liraglutide may reduce the hypoglycemic effects of antidiabetics. Monitoring glycemic control is recommended. 32. Ethinyl Estradiol and Lomitapide: Lomitapide doses should not exceed 30 mg/day when coadministered with ethinyl estradiol. Monitoring is recommended. 33. Ethinyl Estradiol and Lonafarnib: Lonafarnib levels may increase when coadministered with ethinyl estradiol. Nonhormonal contraception is recommended. 34. Ethinyl Estradiol and Metformin: Ethinyl estradiol may reduce the effects of metformin. Monitoring glycemic control is recommended. 35. Ethinyl Estradiol and Mifepristone: Mifepristone may increase ethinyl estradiol levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Alternative therapies are recommended. 36. Ethinyl Estradiol and Minocycline: Minocycline may reduce ethinyl estradiol levels by altering intestinal flora. The risk of contraceptive failure is low, but monitoring is recommended. 37. Ethinyl Estradiol and Mitotane: Mitotane may reduce ethinyl estradiol levels by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitoring is recommended. 38. Ethinyl Estradiol and Mometasone: Mometasone may increase the toxicity of ethinyl estradiol. Monitoring is recommended. 39. Ethinyl Estradiol and Moxifloxacin: Moxifloxacin may reduce ethinyl estradiol levels by altering intestinal flora. The risk of contraceptive failure is low, but monitoring is recommended. 40. Ethinyl Estradiol and Mycophenolate: Mycophenolate may reduce ethinyl estradiol levels through an unknown mechanism. Alternative contraception is recommended. 41. Ethinyl Estradiol and Nafcillin: Nafcillin may reduce ethinyl estradiol levels by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitoring is recommended. 42. Ethinyl Estradiol and Nelfinavir: Nelfinavir may alter ethinyl estradiol levels, potentially reducing contraceptive efficacy. Nonhormonal contraception is recommended. 43. Ethinyl Estradiol and Lixisenatide: Lixisenatide may reduce the absorption of oral contraceptives. Oral contraceptives should be taken at least one hour before or 11 hours after lixisenatide administration. This summary highlights the importance of monitoring and adjusting therapy when ethinyl estradiol is coadministered with other medications.
